title: Cold caller (SDR)
tagline: Learn to open cold calls, handle the top objections and book qualified demos with small business owners.
you_are: an outbound sales development rep for a B2B software company
setting: You dial from a quiet desk or home office, using a dialler and CRM, aiming to reach decision-makers at small businesses during their workday.

scenarios.label: First cold call
scenarios.desc: Reach an owner who answers their own phone and asks why you are calling.
scenarios.setup: You are a small business owner who picked up on the second ring. You sound busy but polite. You say: Who is this and what is this about?
scenarios.objective: Earn thirty seconds to explain the reason for the call and schedule a discovery chat.
scenarios.moment: Tuesday 10:15 am, light office background noise

scenarios.label: Gatekeeper screen
scenarios.desc: Navigate an assistant or spouse who protects the owner’s calendar.
scenarios.setup: You are an executive assistant who answers the main line. You are polite but firm. You say: Can I take a message or would you like to send an email?
scenarios.objective: Get transferred to the owner or secure a specific callback window with the owner’s name.

scenarios.label: Objection cluster
scenarios.desc: Handle the three most common brush-offs in one call without sounding scripted.
scenarios.setup: You are a busy operations manager who has heard five pitches this week. You say: We are not looking right now, we already have a tool, and I do not have budget.
scenarios.objective: Acknowledge each objection, ask one diagnostic question and book a ten-minute discovery call for next week.
scenarios.moment: Thursday 2:05 pm, warehouse hum in background

buyers.angle: Busy, sees no need for new software now.
Worries about hidden costs of software.

buyers.role: owner of a boutique marketing agency
owner of a neighborhood coffee shop

objections: We’re not looking to invest in new software right now
We don’t think we need this kind of tool
Our current system works fine for us
We’re too small to justify a software purchase
I’m not sure this will solve any real problem for us
We prefer to keep things simple and manual
We’ve tried similar solutions before and they failed
We need more proof of results before committing

rubric.label: Opener credibility
rubric.what: State your name, company and a relevant reason for the call in the first two sentences.

rubric.label: Permission ask
rubric.what: Explicitly ask for thirty seconds or a brief moment before launching into value.

rubric.label: Objection curiosity
rubric.what: Acknowledge each brush-off and follow with an open question that uncovers the real concern.

rubric.label: Value tailoring
rubric.what: Connect one concrete outcome to the prospect’s role or industry rather than listing generic features.

rubric.label: Next step clarity
rubric.what: Propose a specific, low-friction next meeting with day, time and duration attached.

rubric.label: Compliance honesty
rubric.what: Identify the call as a sales call, honour do-not-call requests and never misrepresent the product.

pitfalls: Reading a feature list before confirming the prospect’s pain.
Pushing for a demo on the first call instead of a discovery conversation.
Failing to disclose the sales purpose or ignoring a do-not-call request.
line: Cold calling small business owners for a software company

research.text: The top five objections in cold calls account for 74% of all objections, with "no interest or wrong person" and "not thinking about it yet" being common. When faced with these objections, acknowledge them and ask if there's someone else, or frame a follow-up. Cold calling remains effective because it's immediate and personal, cutting through the noise of email and LinkedIn. Handle objections with curiosity, often by asking questions to uncover real concerns. The goal isn't closing a deal on the call but earning the next conversation.
